passage: The science fair started at nine, and the auto was stuck in a traffic jam in the rain. Nilesh, ten, hugged his cardboard water-filter model to his chest, trying to keep it dry. He had built it over three weekends, sanding the funnel and testing it with muddy water until it ran clear. At the school hall one corner was soggy, but it still worked. "Look, sir! Muddy in, clear out!" he said, glowing, and poured a demonstration for every visitor. When Arnab's volcano won first prize, Nilesh cheered loudest. "Your lava went so high!" Later he told his mother, "Next year I'll add a charcoal layer."

qa.q: How many weekends did Nilesh spend building the model?
qa.a: He built it over three weekends.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he poured demonstrations for visitors, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy about his work; he was glowing and wanted to show everyone.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make when Arnab won first prize?
qa.a: He cheered loudest and praised the lava, showing his pride didn't need Arnab to lose.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel hearing Nilesh cheer loudest?
qa.a: Arnab probably felt happy and supported, knowing a friend was truly glad for the win.

grounding: Despite rain and traffic, a ten-year-old glows about a model he worked hard on, shares it eagerly and cheers a friend's win.

passage: In their Kolkata colony's Sunday art class, Leela, eight, had spent a whole month on one drawing: the tram outside her window, every wire and rivet. When she finally finished, she ran to show her Dida, cheeks pink. "Look how I did the shadows!" Dida admired every line. The next Sunday, Rajni's drawing was pinned on the colony notice board. Leela stood in front of it. "Your tram conductor's face is so funny," she told Rajni, grinning. "How did you do the eyes?" Rajni beamed and pulled out her pencil to show her. That evening Leela started a new drawing, the fish market this time, humming.

qa.q: How long did Leela spend on the tram drawing?
qa.a: She spent a whole month on it.

qa.q: What does Leela's "Look how I did the shadows!" show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she is proud of the work she put in and wants to share it.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make when Rajni's drawing was pinned up, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She praised Rajni's drawing and asked how she did the eyes, showing her own pride didn't need Rajni to lose.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when Leela asks how she did the eyes?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and respected, since Leela is genuinely interested in her work.

grounding: An eight-year-old glows over a drawing she worked hard on, is happy for a friend's success and starts her next drawing.

passage:
First Sunday: Sudha wobbled down the lane on her cousin's old cycle and fell three times. Nitin, already riding, showed her how to look ahead, not down.
Second Sunday: She got as far as the tea stall before her foot touched the ground, and she practised every evening that week after homework.
Third Sunday: Sudha rode all the way round the colony park without stopping, bell ringing. "Nitin! Look!" she shouted, glowing. That same day Nitin won the colony race. Sudha cheered loudest of anyone. "Next year I'll race you," she said, "so keep practising."

qa.q: How many times did Sudha fall on the first Sunday?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she shouted "Nitin! Look!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and joyful about a skill she had worked hard for.

qa.q: Why is Sudha's kind of pride healthy?
qa.a: It comes from her own practice, makes her want to keep improving, and leaves room to cheer Nitin's win.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel when Sudha cheers loudest for him?
qa.a: Nitin probably feels happy and supported, especially since he helped her learn.

grounding: Shows a child glowing over a skill earned through practice while happily cheering a friend's success.

passage: When I was ten, beta, I spent a whole monsoon learning to embroider a peacock on a handkerchief. My fingers were full of needle pricks. My Nani made me unpick the neck three times. When it was finally done, I ran through the whole village showing it, even to the postman. I, Aparna, felt like a queen. At the Diwali fair that year my friend Hansa won first prize for her rangoli, and I didn't feel smaller, not one bit. I hugged her and said, "Show me how you did the corners!" My peacock didn't win anything. But I started on a parrot the very next week. That's the kind of proud I want for you.

qa.q: How many times did Nani make Aparna unpick the neck?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did young Aparna feel when the peacock was finished?
qa.a: She felt proud and joyful, like a queen, because of the long work behind it.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows healthy pride?
qa.a: Hugging Hansa and asking to learn her corners, then starting a parrot the next week.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Aparna asked about her corners?
qa.a: Hansa likely felt happy and appreciated, with her friend celebrating instead of competing.

grounding: Shows a child's pride rooted in hard work, happy to share it and glad for a friend's success too.

passage: The power failed ten minutes before the school assembly in Indore, so there'd be no microphone and no fans. Raghav had practised the harmonium tune for three weeks, fingers sore, Nanaji correcting every wrong note. Now he had to play loud enough for the whole hall. He sat down, took a breath and played. Some notes wobbled, but he finished. When he looked up, his face was shining. Afterwards Trisha's dance got the biggest cheer of the morning. Raghav clapped until his palms stung. "Your spins were amazing," he told her. "Did you hear my third line? I finally got it!" Walking home, he was already planning the next song.

qa.q: How long had Raghav practised the harmonium tune?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: How was Raghav feeling when he looked up after playing?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, his face shining because he finished despite the wobbles.

qa.q: Why is Raghav's kind of pride healthy?
qa.a: It comes from real practice, pushes him towards the next song and doesn't stop him cheering for Trisha.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel when Raghav praises her spins?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels pleased and warm, seeing that he is glad for her as well as himself.

grounding: Illustrates a child's pride in a skill earned through practice, shared gladly and alongside joy for a friend.

passage:
Uday burst into the Kolkata flat waving a paper kite. "Maa! I made it myself! Look, the tail doesn't wobble anymore."
It had taken him four tries. The first three had torn or spun into the neighbour's balcony. This one had flown above the water tank for ten whole minutes.
He ran down to the rooftop again to show his friend Gurleen. She had brought her own kite, a shiny blue one, and hers flew even higher.
"Whoa, yours is so high!" Uday shouted, grinning. "How did you tie the string?"
Gurleen showed him the knot. Uday tried it on his kite, and it rose a little higher too.
That night he drew plans for a bigger kite, with a longer tail.

qa.q: How many tries did it take Uday to make the kite?
qa.a: Four tries.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when his kite finally flew?
qa.a: He felt proud and joyful; he burst into the flat waving it and wanted to show everyone.

qa.q: What does Uday's reaction to Gurleen's kite show about healthy pride?
qa.a: He was happy for her and asked how she tied the string, so his pride didn't need her to lose, and he learned something new.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when Uday cheers for her kite?
qa.a: Gurleen would likely feel glad and friendly, happy to share her knot with someone who is excited for her.

grounding: Shows a child glowing with pride in a kite he worked hard on, sharing it and celebrating a friend's success too.
